hints: Calculate the work done by the driving force over $50\text{ m}$: $W_{\text{driving}} = F \times d = 100 \times 50 = 5000\text{ J}$.
Apply the work-energy principle: net work done equals kinetic energy gained, so $W_{\text{driving}} - W_{\text{resistance}} = \frac{1}{2}m v^2$.
walkthrough:
Calculate the work done by the cyclist's constant driving force:
$$W_{\text{driving}} = 100 \times 50 = 5000\text{ J}$$

Form the work-energy balance equation with $u = 0$, $v = 6\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $W_{\text{resistance}} = 3560\text{ J}$:
$$W_{\text{driving}} - W_{\text{resistance}} = \frac{1}{2}m v^2$$
$$5000 - 3560 = \frac{1}{2}m(6^2)$$
$$1440 = 18m$$

Solve for the total mass $m$:
$$m = \frac{1440}{18} = 80\text{ kg}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
State the work-energy theorem for horizontal motion:
$$\text{Net work done} = \Delta KE$$
$$W_{\text{driving}} - W_{\text{resistance}} = \frac{1}{2}m v^2 - \frac{1}{2}m u^2$$
Identify the parameters from the problem:
- Distance travelled: $d = 50\text{ m}$
- Constant driving force: $F = 100\text{ N}$
- Work against resistance: $W_{\text{resistance}} = 3560\text{ J}$
- Initial speed: $u = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ (starts from rest)
- Final speed: $v = 6\text{ m s}^{-1}$

Calculate the work done by the driving force:
$$W_{\text{driving}} = F \times d = 100 \times 50 = 5000\text{ J}$$

Compute the net work done on the cyclist and bicycle:
$$W_{\text{net}} = 5000 - 3560 = 1440\text{ J}$$

Equate net work to the kinetic energy gained:
$$1440 = \frac{1}{2}m(6^2)$$
$$6^2 = 36$$
$$1440 = \frac{1}{2}m(36) = 18m$$

Divide both sides by $18$:
$$m = \frac{1440}{18} = 80\text{ kg}$$
Thus, the total mass of the cyclist and bicycle is $80\text{ kg}$.
